abstract: Summary Polyamines play crucial roles in modulating T lymphocyte functions. Here, we demonstrate that the oral mucosa of people living with HIV (PLWH), characterized by active polyamine metabolic pathways, exhibits significantly diminished IFN-γ expression and reduced abundance of CD8 + tissue-resident memory (T RM ) cells. Salivary 16S rRNA sequencing revealed elevated levels of Fusobacteria, negatively correlating with the levels of CD8 + T RM -like cells in PLWH. In vitro experiments showed that Fusobacterium nucleatum (FN) produced putrescine, which is known to be enriched in PLWH mucosa. Polyamines, HIV infection, and FN led to EIF-5A hypusination, diminished IFN-γ expression in CD8 + T cells, which impaired the proliferation of TRM-like cells in tonsil organoid cells. The inhibition of polyamine synthesis and EIF-5A hypusination restored IFN-γ expression and T RM -like cells. Collectively, these results highlight an essential role of polyamines in the critical interplay between oral resident microbiota, immunometabolic regulation, and immune competence during chronic viral infections.

Fusobacterium cultures and lysate preparation
Fusobacterium nucleatum subsp. nucleatum
ATCC 25586 was grown under anaerobic conditions at 37°C for 18 h in different broth media in glass test tubes in triplicates.

Undefined media included Tryptic Soy broth (Fisher Scientific) supplemented 0.5% yeast extract (Sigma) and 1% peptone (Thomas Scientific) (TSBYEP) with or without 10 mM ornithine. Defined media included oral chemically defined media containing 20 mM D-glucose and 10 mM D-sucrose with 1M 3-(N-morpholino) propane sulfonic acid and prepared without polyamines, with or without 10 mM ornithine.

After cultures were grown, supernatants and lysates were prepared as follows. All cultures were centrifuged at 4000 x g for 10 min to separate supernatants from cell pellets. Supernatants were passed through a 0.2 μm filter to remove any cellular debris. The cell pellets were washed twice in 1x phosphate-buffered saline (pH 7.4) and resuspended in extraction buffer (50 mM Trizma base, 0.1 mM EDTA, and 1 mM 2-mercaptoethanol [pH 7.5]). Cells were then mechanically lysed with 0.1 mm zirconium beads for 30 seconds three times using the Bead Ruptor 24 (Omni International, Inc). Cell lysates were centrifuged at 4 C° at 16,000 x g for 2 min. Supernatants of lysed cells were passed through a 0.2 μm filter to remove any remaining cell debris or un-lysed cells. Media controls without FN growth were included for comparison.

Supernatants and lysates were stored at -20 C° until LC-MS analysis or cell culture usage.
Sample collection and DNA extraction for 16SrRNA sequencing
Bacterial DNA Isolation
: Bacterial DNA was extracted from 50 uL of saliva per sample using QIAamp PowerFecal Pro DNA Kit (Qiagen) and following the provided manufacturer protocol. ZymoBIOMICS™ Microbial Community Standard (Zymo Research Corporation) and UltraPure™ DNase/RNase-Free Distilled Water (Invitrogen) were used as positive and negative controls respectively and were processed in parallel with the samples.
16S rRNA sequencing
: PCR amplification was performed using primers that targeted the V4 region of the 16S gene: 5’- GTG CCA GCM GCC GCG GTA A-3’ for the forward primer and 5’- GGA CTA CHV GGG TWT CTA AT-3’ for the reverse primer. The PCR reaction was done in a reaction well plate using 5 ul template DNA, 2.5 ul Gold Buffer (10X), 2.5 ul MgCl2 (25 mM), 0.5 dNTP (10 mM), 1 ul each of the forward and reverse primers (10 uM), 0.25 ul AmpliTaq Gold DNA Polymerase (5 U/ul), and 12.25 ul UltraPure DNase/RNase-free distilled water (Invitrogen). The PCR amplification conditions were set to the following settings: 95C for 3 minutes, then 28 cycles of 95C for 30 seconds, 55C for 30 seconds, and 72C for 30 seconds, then finishing at 72C for 5 minutes. Amplicons were then purified using Ampure XP Beads and confirmed with the TapeStation 4150 (Agilent). DNA was quantified using Quant-iT™ dsDNA Assay Kits HS (Invitrogen) and normalized to 4 nM. The pooled library was diluted to 8 pM with 10% spike-in of 12.5 pM PhiX before running on the Illumina MiSeq, using 500 cycles v2 PE reagents, yielding 2 x 250 bp paired-end reads (Illumina).
16S rRNA data processing
: Sequence reads were analyzed for quality control with the DADA2 pipeline (version 1.26). Pair-end reads for each sample were assembled into contigs and primer sequences were trimmed. Sequences were classified using the Ribosomal Database Project (RDP) taxonomy database (version 16). Taxa that were detected at higher average levels in the negative water controls relative to the samples were removed as contaminants. OTUs were assigned based on their most specific taxa hits prior to downstream analysis. OTUs were categorized as “undistinguishable” if the database is unable to classify the sequence beyond domain or class. Low abundance taxa were binned to “other” if it accounted for < 0.025% of total species detected across all samples.
Quality control
: Sequence quality control and denoising were performed using QIIME 2 (v2024.5),
49
an open-source bioinformatics pipeline for microbiome analysis. Low-quality bases (quality score < 30) at the sequence ends were trimmed, and sequences shorter than 100 nucleotides were excluded. The DADA2
48
plugin was applied to filter and correct sequencing errors, infer amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), and remove chimeric sequences. Specifically, the first 15 bases of both forward and reverse reads were trimmed to remove primers and low-quality regions, while forward and reverse reads were truncated at 240 bp and 220 bp, respectively to retain high-quality regions. This procedure ensured the removal of sequencing errors while preserving high-resolution ASVs for downstream taxonomic and diversity analyses.
Taxonomy assignment
: To minimize sequencing noise and consolidate similar sequences,
de novo
operational taxonomic unit (OTU) clustering was performed using VSEARCH within QIIME 2. Sequences were clustered at 99% sequence identity, grouping highly similar sequences into the same OTU. For bacterial microbiome analysis, filtered amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were taxonomically classified using the QIIME 2 feature-classifier plugin, which applies a naïve Bayes classifier trained on the SILVA reference database.
57
SILVA is a widely recognized, high-quality ribosomal RNA (rRNA) reference database that enables accurate taxonomic annotation of microbial communities.
52
Taxonomic assignment was performed using the pre-trained naïve Bayes classifier based on SILVA release 138, with a 99% sequence identity threshold. The resulting OTU tables and taxonomy assignments were integrated into two phyloseq objects
58
in .RData format for downstream statistical and visualization analyses. The phyloseq framework facilitates streamlined microbiome data management, supporting efficient implementation of alpha diversity, beta diversity, and differential abundance analyses.
Alpha Diversity Analysis
: Alpha diversity was assessed using two metrics: the Shannon index and the Chao1 richness estimator. The Shannon index incorporates both species richness and evenness, providing a measure of diversity within each sample, while the Chao1 index estimates species richness, particularly accounting for rare taxa. These metrics were computed for each sample using R (v4.4.1) vegan package, and differences in alpha diversity were evaluated between the two groups. Statistical significance was assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test, a non-parametric method suitable for comparing distributions between two independent groups. Multiple testing corrections were applied where appropriate to control for false discovery rates.
Beta Diversity Analysis:
Beta diversity was assessed to compare microbial community composition across samples using the weighted UniFrac distance metric,
59
a phylogenetic-based measure that accounts for both taxonomic relatedness and relative abundance. The weighted UniFrac distances were computed using the GUniFrac package in R. To evaluate differences in microbial community composition between HIV+ and HIV− groups, permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) was performed on pairwise weighted UniFrac distances using the adonis2 function from the ape package in R, with 999 permutations. To visualize the beta diversity patterns, principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was conducted on the weighted UniFrac distance matrix using the cmd scale function from the R base package. The first two principal coordinate axes were plotted to capture the major sources of variation in microbial community structure across samples.
Differential Abundance Analysis
:
To identify microbial taxa that significantly differed between the two groups, differential abundance analysis was conducted using the Linear Discriminant Analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) method.
60
LEfSe is a statistical approach designed to detect biologically meaningful differences in microbiome composition by integrating non-parametric statistical tests with Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). LEfSe analysis was performed using the microbiome Marker package in R. For microbiome data, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (for two-group comparisons) and the Kruskal-Wallis test (for multi-group comparisons) were applied with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. The LDA score cutoff was set to 2.0 to ensure the selection of strongly discriminative microbial features. To control for multiple testing, p-values were adjusted using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. To visualize the hierarchical structure of microbial biomarkers identified by LEfSe, a taxonomy tree was constructed using the BAZE package. This representation facilitates the interpretation of taxonomic relationships among differentially abundant microbial taxa. For the key microbial markers identified through LEfSe analysis, we further examined their association with Control and PLWH groups using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. To ensure robust statistical inference, p-values were adjusted using both FDR correction and Bonferroni adjustment, minimizing the risk of false-positive findings. This stringent approach enhances the reliability of conclusions regarding the significance of microbial differences between the groups in comparison.
RNA sequencing
Sample preparation, sequencing, alignment, and analyses were performed by Novogene. Strand-specific libraries were generated using the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq2500 (TruSeq V4 chemistry) with a paired-end 150 bp protocol (PE150). Raw reads (125 bp paired-end FASTQ files) were trimmed with Trimmomatic v0.30 to remove adapters and aligned to the human genome using STAR v2.5 with the GENCODE v4 (Ensembl 78) annotation. Gene counts from gingival biopsies (three biological replicates) were normalized with limma v3.26.8 and analyzed by unpaired
t
-test. Normalized counts were converted to RPKM values for heatmap visualization.
Salivary metabolomics
Sample collection: Human saliva samples were collected in 50 mL sterile tubes and stored at −80 °C.

For LC-MS analysis (Creative Proteomics), 100 μL frozen aliquots were thawed, transferred to new tubes, and extracted with 200 μL of 80% methanol. Samples were vortexed (30 s), incubated at −40 °C for 1 h, vortexed again (30 s), and centrifuged (10,000 g, 4 °C, 15 min). 200 μL of supernatant and 5 μL of internal standard (DL-o-Chlorophenylalanine, 1 mg/mL) were transferred to vials. Quality control (QC) samples were prepared by pooling equal amounts of extracts from all samples and processed identically.
Instrumental setup: Analysis was performed on an Ultimate 3000LC coupled to a Q Exactive MS (Thermo) using ESI-MS in targeted MS/MS mode. Chromatographic separation was achieved with an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm) at 40 °C and a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min. The mobile phase consisted of solvent A (0.05% formic acid in water) and solvent B (acetonitrile) with a gradient: 0–1.0 min, 95% A; 1.0–12.0 min, 95%–5% A; 12.0–13.5 min, 5% A; 13.5–13.6 min, 5%–95% A; 13.6–16 min, 95% A. The sample manager was maintained at 4 °C.

Targeted polyamine quantification in bacterial and cellular lysates using LC-MS
Sample preparation
Serially diluted standard solutions of the five polyamines were prepared in 10% acetonitrile. Cell lysates and supernatants from three independent experiments were processed and analyzed separately. For derivatization, 40 μL of each thawed supernatant or standard solution was mixed with 80 μL of 20 mM dansyl chloride solution and 20 μL of borate buffer and incubated at 40 °C for 30 minutes. UPLC-MRM/MS analysis was performed at Creative Proteomics: 10 μL of each derivatized sample was injected onto a C18 column (2.1 × 150 mm, 1.8 μm) and separated on an Agilent 1290 UHPLC system coupled to an Agilent 6495B QQQ mass spectrometer in positive-ion mode. A binary gradient of 0.1% formic acid in water (A) and acetonitrile (B) was used (50% to 100% B in 15 min) at a flow rate of 0.35 mL/min and 55 °C.
Quantification and statistical analysis
A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. P-values were calculated using Prism 8 (GraphPad Software). For comparisons of random distributions, the Mann-Whitney test was used, while one-way or two-way ANOVA was employed for multiple group comparisons. To examine changes between groups, the unpaired two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test was utilized and Bonferroni t-tests served as post hoc tests for multiple comparisons. For correlation analyses, an alpha value < 0.05 was considered significant, and Spearman correlation (r) as well as simple linear regression (R
2
) were calculated.

After cultures were grown, supernatants and lysates were prepared as follows. All cultures were centrifuged at 4000 x g for 10 min to separate supernatants from cell pellets. Supernatants were passed through a 0.2 μm filter to remove any cellular debris. The cell pellets were washed twice in 1x phosphate-buffered saline (pH 7.4) and resuspended in extraction buffer (50 mM Trizma base, 0.1 mM EDTA, and 1 mM 2-mercaptoethanol [pH 7.5]). Cells were then mechanically lysed with 0.1 mm zirconium beads for 30 seconds three times using the Bead Ruptor 24 (Omni International, Inc). Cell lysates were centrifuged at 4 C° at 16,000 x g for 2 min. Supernatants of lysed cells were passed through a 0.2 μm filter to remove any remaining cell debris or un-lysed cells. Media controls without FN growth were included for comparison.
26
Supernatants and lysates were stored at -20 C° until LC-MS analysis or cell culture usage.
Sample collection and DNA extraction for 16SrRNA sequencing
Bacterial DNA Isolation
: Bacterial DNA was extracted from 50 uL of saliva per sample using QIAamp PowerFecal Pro DNA Kit (Qiagen) and following the provided manufacturer protocol. ZymoBIOMICS™ Microbial Community Standard (Zymo Research Corporation) and UltraPure™ DNase/RNase-Free Distilled Water (Invitrogen) were used as positive and negative controls respectively and were processed in parallel with the samples.
16S rRNA sequencing
: PCR amplification was performed using primers that targeted the V4 region of the 16S gene: 5’- GTG CCA GCM GCC GCG GTA A-3’ for the forward primer and 5’- GGA CTA CHV GGG TWT CTA AT-3’ for the reverse primer. The PCR reaction was done in a reaction well plate using 5 ul template DNA, 2.5 ul Gold Buffer (10X), 2.5 ul MgCl2 (25 mM), 0.5 dNTP (10 mM), 1 ul each of the forward and reverse primers (10 uM), 0.25 ul AmpliTaq Gold DNA Polymerase (5 U/ul), and 12.25 ul UltraPure DNase/RNase-free distilled water (Invitrogen). The PCR amplification conditions were set to the following settings: 95C for 3 minutes, then 28 cycles of 95C for 30 seconds, 55C for 30 seconds, and 72C for 30 seconds, then finishing at 72C for 5 minutes. Amplicons were then purified using Ampure XP Beads and confirmed with the TapeStation 4150 (Agilent). DNA was quantified using Quant-iT™ dsDNA Assay Kits HS (Invitrogen) and normalized to 4 nM. The pooled library was diluted to 8 pM with 10% spike-in of 12.5 pM PhiX before running on the Illumina MiSeq, using 500 cycles v2 PE reagents, yielding 2 x 250 bp paired-end reads (Illumina).
16S rRNA data processing
: Sequence reads were analyzed for quality control with the DADA2 pipeline (version 1.26). Pair-end reads for each sample were assembled into contigs and primer sequences were trimmed. Sequences were classified using the Ribosomal Database Project (RDP) taxonomy database (version 16). Taxa that were detected at higher average levels in the negative water controls relative to the samples were removed as contaminants. OTUs were assigned based on their most specific taxa hits prior to downstream analysis. OTUs were categorized as “undistinguishable” if the database is unable to classify the sequence beyond domain or class. Low abundance taxa were binned to “other” if it accounted for < 0.025% of total species detected across all samples.
Quality control
: Sequence quality control and denoising were performed using QIIME 2 (v2024.5),
49
an open-source bioinformatics pipeline for microbiome analysis. Low-quality bases (quality score < 30) at the sequence ends were trimmed, and sequences shorter than 100 nucleotides were excluded. The DADA2
48
plugin was applied to filter and correct sequencing errors, infer amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), and remove chimeric sequences. Specifically, the first 15 bases of both forward and reverse reads were trimmed to remove primers and low-quality regions, while forward and reverse reads were truncated at 240 bp and 220 bp, respectively to retain high-quality regions. This procedure ensured the removal of sequencing errors while preserving high-resolution ASVs for downstream taxonomic and diversity analyses.
Taxonomy assignment
: To minimize sequencing noise and consolidate similar sequences,
de novo
operational taxonomic unit (OTU) clustering was performed using VSEARCH within QIIME 2. Sequences were clustered at 99% sequence identity, grouping highly similar sequences into the same OTU. For bacterial microbiome analysis, filtered amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were taxonomically classified using the QIIME 2 feature-classifier plugin, which applies a naïve Bayes classifier trained on the SILVA reference database.
57
SILVA is a widely recognized, high-quality ribosomal RNA (rRNA) reference database that enables accurate taxonomic annotation of microbial communities.
52
Taxonomic assignment was performed using the pre-trained naïve Bayes classifier based on SILVA release 138, with a 99% sequence identity threshold. The resulting OTU tables and taxonomy assignments were integrated into two phyloseq objects
58
in .RData format for downstream statistical and visualization analyses. The phyloseq framework facilitates streamlined microbiome data management, supporting efficient implementation of alpha diversity, beta diversity, and differential abundance analyses.
Alpha Diversity Analysis
: Alpha diversity was assessed using two metrics: the Shannon index and the Chao1 richness estimator. The Shannon index incorporates both species richness and evenness, providing a measure of diversity within each sample, while the Chao1 index estimates species richness, particularly accounting for rare taxa. These metrics were computed for each sample using R (v4.4.1) vegan package, and differences in alpha diversity were evaluated between the two groups. Statistical significance was assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test, a non-parametric method suitable for comparing distributions between two independent groups. Multiple testing corrections were applied where appropriate to control for false discovery rates.
Beta Diversity Analysis:
Beta diversity was assessed to compare microbial community composition across samples using the weighted UniFrac distance metric,
59
a phylogenetic-based measure that accounts for both taxonomic relatedness and relative abundance. The weighted UniFrac distances were computed using the GUniFrac package in R. To evaluate differences in microbial community composition between HIV+ and HIV− groups, permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) was performed on pairwise weighted UniFrac distances using the adonis2 function from the ape package in R, with 999 permutations. To visualize the beta diversity patterns, principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was conducted on the weighted UniFrac distance matrix using the cmd scale function from the R base package. The first two principal coordinate axes were plotted to capture the major sources of variation in microbial community structure across samples.
Differential Abundance Analysis
:
To identify microbial taxa that significantly differed between the two groups, differential abundance analysis was conducted using the Linear Discriminant Analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) method.
60
LEfSe is a statistical approach designed to detect biologically meaningful differences in microbiome composition by integrating non-parametric statistical tests with Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). LEfSe analysis was performed using the microbiome Marker package in R. For microbiome data, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (for two-group comparisons) and the Kruskal-Wallis test (for multi-group comparisons) were applied with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. The LDA score cutoff was set to 2.0 to ensure the selection of strongly discriminative microbial features. To control for multiple testing, p-values were adjusted using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. To visualize the hierarchical structure of microbial biomarkers identified by LEfSe, a taxonomy tree was constructed using the BAZE package. This representation facilitates the interpretation of taxonomic relationships among differentially abundant microbial taxa. For the key microbial markers identified through LEfSe analysis, we further examined their association with Control and PLWH groups using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. To ensure robust statistical inference, p-values were adjusted using both FDR correction and Bonferroni adjustment, minimizing the risk of false-positive findings. This stringent approach enhances the reliability of conclusions regarding the significance of microbial differences between the groups in comparison.
RNA sequencing
Sample preparation, sequencing, alignment, and analyses were performed by Novogene. Strand-specific libraries were generated using the NEBNext® Ultra™ RNA Library Prep Kit and sequenced on an Illumina HiSeq2500 (TruSeq V4 chemistry) with a paired-end 150 bp protocol (PE150). Raw reads (125 bp paired-end FASTQ files) were trimmed with Trimmomatic v0.30 to remove adapters and aligned to the human genome using STAR v2.5 with the GENCODE v4 (Ensembl 78) annotation. Gene counts from gingival biopsies (three biological replicates) were normalized with limma v3.26.8 and analyzed by unpaired
t
-test. Normalized counts were converted to RPKM values for heatmap visualization.
Salivary metabolomics
Sample collection: Human saliva samples were collected in 50 mL sterile tubes and stored at −80 °C.
4
,
5
For LC-MS analysis (Creative Proteomics), 100 μL frozen aliquots were thawed, transferred to new tubes, and extracted with 200 μL of 80% methanol. Samples were vortexed (30 s), incubated at −40 °C for 1 h, vortexed again (30 s), and centrifuged (10,000 g, 4 °C, 15 min). 200 μL of supernatant and 5 μL of internal standard (DL-o-Chlorophenylalanine, 1 mg/mL) were transferred to vials. Quality control (QC) samples were prepared by pooling equal amounts of extracts from all samples and processed identically.
Instrumental setup: Analysis was performed on an Ultimate 3000LC coupled to a Q Exactive MS (Thermo) using ESI-MS in targeted MS/MS mode. Chromatographic separation was achieved with an ACQUITY UPLC HSS T3 column (100 × 2.1 mm, 1.8 μm) at 40 °C and a flow rate of 0.3 mL/min. The mobile phase consisted of solvent A (0.05% formic acid in water) and solvent B (acetonitrile) with a gradient: 0–1.0 min, 95% A; 1.0–12.0 min, 95%–5% A; 12.0–13.5 min, 5% A; 13.5–13.6 min, 5%–95% A; 13.6–16 min, 95% A. The sample manager was maintained at 4 °C.

ESI+: Heater Temp 300 °C; Sheath Gas 45 arb; Aux Gas 15 arb; Sweep Gas 1 arb; Spray Voltage 3.0 kV; Capillary Temp 350 °C; S-Lens RF 30%.
ESI−: Heater Temp 300 °C; Sheath Gas 45 arb; Aux Gas 15 arb; Sweep Gas 1 arb; Spray Voltage 3.2 kV; Capillary Temp 350 °C; S-Lens RF 60%.
Bioinformatics analysis: Data analysis included multivariate and single-variable analyses, clustering, and correlation network construction of differential metabolites. Metabolite identifications were made using Compound Discoverer 3.1 SP1 and MZmine2 softwares in our previous study.
5
MS1 and MS2 spectra were matched using a mass tolerance of m/z = 0.1.

Sample preparation
Serially diluted standard solutions of the five polyamines were prepared in 10% acetonitrile. Cell lysates and supernatants from three independent experiments were processed and analyzed separately. For derivatization, 40 μL of each thawed supernatant or standard solution was mixed with 80 μL of 20 mM dansyl chloride solution and 20 μL of borate buffer and incubated at 40 °C for 30 minutes. UPLC-MRM/MS analysis was performed at Creative Proteomics: 10 μL of each derivatized sample was injected onto a C18 column (2.1 × 150 mm, 1.8 μm) and separated on an Agilent 1290 UHPLC system coupled to an Agilent 6495B QQQ mass spectrometer in positive-ion mode. A binary gradient of 0.1% formic acid in water (A) and acetonitrile (B) was used (50% to 100% B in 15 min) at a flow rate of 0.35 mL/min and 55 °C.

Discussion
Polyamine-mediated modulation of CD8
+
tissue-resident memory cells in chronic HIV infection: Implications of dysbiosis
CD8
+
tissue-resident memory (T
RM
) cells are pivotal for local immune defense at mucosal barrier sites. This study elucidates the polyamine-mediated effects on CD8
+
TRM cell impairment caused by dysbiosis during chronic HIV infection. Our results support the idea that HIV-associated dysbiosis, marked by increased
Fusobacterium
abundance, enhances bacterial putrescine production within the mucosal niche, contributing to T
reg
dysfunction as well as to the loss of T
RM
cells. Employing a multifaceted approach—integrating metabolomics, 16S rRNA sequencing, flow cytometry, and functional assays, this study has explored the role of polyamines in modulating CD8
+
T cell functions. Acute HIV infection coincides with the infiltration of CD4
+
and CD8
+
T cells into mucosal sites, leading to epithelial cell apoptosis and mucosal barrier defects.
29
Our previous research indicated no significant changes in CD4/CD8 ratios or frequencies in the oral mucosa of cART-treated chronic HIV-positive individuals.
4
,
5
However, characterization of the CD8
+
population in this study, using the same cohort reveals a reduced frequency of a subset of CD8
+
T cells, i.e.,
.
, CD8
+
T
RM
cells in their oral mucosa compared to uninfected controls (
Figure 1
). Consistent with prior findings that showed exhaustion in HIV-specific CD8
+
T
RM-
like in HIV-infected individuals,
30
,
31
,
32
we also observed increased PD-1 expression, reduced IFN-γ in CD8
+
T cells in PLWH in the gingival mucosa (
Figure 1
). These data suggest that CD8
+
cells found in PLWH exhibit impaired effector functions and might also contribute to the decline in T
RM
cells. RNA sequencing revealed partial exhaustion and apoptotic signatures in PLWH (
Figure 1
J); however, a complete CD8
+
T
RM
-cell exhaustion signature could not be specifically assessed due to the limited size of gingival biopsy samples. Future single-cell RNA sequencing will be essential to define the precise phenotypes of individual T cell subsets within the oral mucosa.
Our study further provides deeper mechanistic insights into the role of polyamines in modulating CD8
+
T cell functions within the framework of mucosal dysbiosis. Polyamines upregulated EIF5A hypusination in CD8
+
T cells, leading to reduced expression of IFN-γ and key T
RM
signature markers (
Figures 2
and
3
). This aligns with previous research demonstrating that these metabolites modulate the cytolytic function of CD8
+
T cells and some features of memory development.
10
,
33

+
T
RM
like cells (
Figures S4
,
S5
, and
3
). Because IFN-γ neutralization also led to a loss of T
RM
-like cells
in vitro
(
Figure 3
), we propose that effector IFN-γ provides a feedforward mechanism that promotes the induction and proliferation of T
RM
cells,
13
which can be inhibited by excessive polyamines.
While our previous research identified polyamine metabolism as a driver of immunometabolic alterations in mucosal CD4
+
cells,
4
,
5
given that resident microbiota are substantial sources of polyamines,

,

this study explored the potential impact of oral microbial dysbiosis in PLWH. Comprehensive microbiome analysis revealed dysbiosis in PLWH, with elevated
Fusobacteria
abundance correlating with putrescine levels (

our study futher demonstrated increased abundance of

in polyamine dysregulation
.

Limitations of the study
Our results favor the notion that the increase in CD4
+
T
regs
is at least partially attributed to the heightened abundance of
Fusobacteria
in PLWH. However, based on
in vitro
experiments, it is unlikely that the increase in CD4
+
T
regs
is mediated directly by polyamines (
4
,
5
Figure S3
). These findings suggest that chronic HIV infection in PLWH disrupts polyamine regulation directly in host CD4
+
T cells,
4
,
5
as well as indirectly through dysbiosis. High
Fusobacterium
levels in PLWH may independently promote FOXP3
+
cell induction or recruitment in the mucosa through mechanisms not yet fully understood and remain to be determined in the future. Nevertheless, our results suggest that
Fusobacteria
may not only elevate CD4
+
T
regs
but also be involved in T
reg
dysfunction and AREG expression in CD4
+
T
regs
(
Figures S12
and
S13
) in PLWH. Next, gingival mucosal CD8
+
T cells in PLWH exhibited lower levels of BCL-2—an anti-apoptotic protein—suggesting reduced cell viability of T
RM
cells compared to controls
in vivo
(
Figures 1
H and 1I), but neither HIV nor FN exposure led to BCL-2 downregulation in CD8
+
T cells in HTOC cultures (
Figure S17
). Thus, PLWH data link CD8
+
T
RM
loss to exhaustion and apoptotic programs (
Figure 1
J), while
in vitro
HIV infection points to impaired proliferation. Finally, the cytokine loss in CD8
+
T
RM
-like cells in polyamine and HIV-infected cultures did not associate with PD-1 upregulation
in vitro
. Polyamines, HIV, and FN did not consistently and significantly modulate PD-1 expression across the experiments, despite their ability to downregulate cytokines (
Figures S4
,
S5
,
S10
, and
8
). These data imply that PD1 expression is modulated differently in
invitro
activated T cells, which are significantly distinct from those in chronically activated milieu in gingival tissues of PLWH. Taken together, the results highlight certain limitations of
in vitro
models of acute HIV infection in accurately replicating the mucosal environment observed in chronic and treated HIV infection, especially when dysbiosis in the mucosa is also a contributing factor. Both PLWH and HTOC data, however, converge on reduced IFN-γ as a common mechanism underlying CD8
+
T
RM
loss.
FN consistently induced diminished expression of IFN-γ and T
RM
-like markers without affecting the activation of CD8
+
T cells both in uninfected and HIV-infected cells (
Figure 7
). Similar to PLWH, which showed diminished T
RM
cells in the oral mucosa, the additive effects of FN and HIV significantly tempered T
RM
-like cells
in vitro
(
Figure 7
). Because FN is the most prevalent species of
Fusobacteria
in the oral cavity,
37
we performed the
in vitro
experiments with FN. Although polyamine metabolism supports FN growth and putrescine synthesis (
Figure 5
), our results do not rule out the possibility that it may vary among different strains of
Fusobacteria
. Some
Fusobacterium
species can utilize alternative metabolic pathways under nutrient-limited conditions, depending on unique interactions within microbial communities within the oral cavity. Nevertheless, our data suggests that HIV infection and subsequent dysbiosis involving
Fusobacteria
abundance lead to polyamine enrichment and T
RM
cell loss in PLWH. As expected, these additive effects mechanistically require T cell polyamine metabolism and synthesis, as both DFMO and GC7 partially restore the proliferation and cytokine expression of T
RM
-like cells (
Figures S4
,
S5
, and
8
).
We also acknowledge other limitations in our study, such as the relatively small cohort size, the inability of our methods to resolve the bacteriome at the species level, and employing cART-treated PLWH that may confound HIV-specific effects. Nonetheless, our findings strongly support the hypothesis that dysbiosis, in conjunction with chronic infection in treated HIV infection, contributes to polyamine-dependent immuno-metabolic dysfunction in oral mucosal T cells. While we hypothesize that residual mucosal inflammation-associated cytokines and antigen-independent activation of immune cells, including hyperactivated CD4
+
T cells in treated HIV infection, contribute to T
RM
attrition during chronic HIV disease, we currently lack data to support this tenet fully. We did not confirm whether the CD8
+
T
RM
cells identified are HIV-reactive in PLWH. Further investigation is required to elucidate whether T
RM
cells are HIV-reactive and the role of antiretroviral therapy in altering microbiome composition. Given that CXCR6 facilitates survival of CD8
+
T cells within the tumor microenvironment,
38
the diminished frequency of CXCR6
+
CD8
+
T
RM
cells may impair tumor immunity in HIV-positive patients. Also, considering the role of polyamines
39
and oral
Fusobacterium nucleatum
in cancers,
37
,
40
,
41
it is tempting to speculate that
Fusobacterium
abundance and T
RM
decline in mucosa may contribute to increased cancer predisposition in PLWH.
42
,
43
Future studies are required to validate this tenet.
In conclusion, polyamines produced by resident microbiota and host mucosal cells are absorbed and metabolized by immune cells, maintaining normal immune mucosal homeostasis. Dysbiosis, in the context of a chronic infection, disrupts this balance, leading to T cell dysfunction. Thus, chronic immune diseases such as HIV infection, despite antiretroviral therapy, coupled with dysbiosis, may contribute to T cell dysfunction by elevating mucosal polyamines, impairing IFN-γ production and CD8
+
T
RM
responses. Therefore, this study underscores the vital role of polyamines in the intricate interplay between microbial composition, immunometabolic regulation, and hypofunctional states in CD8
+
T cells. It also uncovers novel opportunities to regulate polyamine pathways for modulating T cell responses, thereby offering potential strategies for treating chronic inflammation and dysbiosis.

Sample collection and DNA extraction for 16SrRNA sequencing
Bacterial DNA Isolation
: Bacterial DNA was extracted from 50 uL of saliva per sample using QIAamp PowerFecal Pro DNA Kit (Qiagen) and following the provided manufacturer protocol. ZymoBIOMICS™ Microbial Community Standard (Zymo Research Corporation) and UltraPure™ DNase/RNase-Free Distilled Water (Invitrogen) were used as positive and negative controls respectively and were processed in parallel with the samples.
16S rRNA sequencing
: PCR amplification was performed using primers that targeted the V4 region of the 16S gene: 5’- GTG CCA GCM GCC GCG GTA A-3’ for the forward primer and 5’- GGA CTA CHV GGG TWT CTA AT-3’ for the reverse primer. The PCR reaction was done in a reaction well plate using 5 ul template DNA, 2.5 ul Gold Buffer (10X), 2.5 ul MgCl2 (25 mM), 0.5 dNTP (10 mM), 1 ul each of the forward and reverse primers (10 uM), 0.25 ul AmpliTaq Gold DNA Polymerase (5 U/ul), and 12.25 ul UltraPure DNase/RNase-free distilled water (Invitrogen). The PCR amplification conditions were set to the following settings: 95C for 3 minutes, then 28 cycles of 95C for 30 seconds, 55C for 30 seconds, and 72C for 30 seconds, then finishing at 72C for 5 minutes. Amplicons were then purified using Ampure XP Beads and confirmed with the TapeStation 4150 (Agilent). DNA was quantified using Quant-iT™ dsDNA Assay Kits HS (Invitrogen) and normalized to 4 nM. The pooled library was diluted to 8 pM with 10% spike-in of 12.5 pM PhiX before running on the Illumina MiSeq, using 500 cycles v2 PE reagents, yielding 2 x 250 bp paired-end reads (Illumina).
16S rRNA data processing
: Sequence reads were analyzed for quality control with the DADA2 pipeline (version 1.26). Pair-end reads for each sample were assembled into contigs and primer sequences were trimmed. Sequences were classified using the Ribosomal Database Project (RDP) taxonomy database (version 16). Taxa that were detected at higher average levels in the negative water controls relative to the samples were removed as contaminants. OTUs were assigned based on their most specific taxa hits prior to downstream analysis. OTUs were categorized as “undistinguishable” if the database is unable to classify the sequence beyond domain or class. Low abundance taxa were binned to “other” if it accounted for < 0.025% of total species detected across all samples.
Quality control
: Sequence quality control and denoising were performed using QIIME 2 (v2024.5),
49
an open-source bioinformatics pipeline for microbiome analysis. Low-quality bases (quality score < 30) at the sequence ends were trimmed, and sequences shorter than 100 nucleotides were excluded. The DADA2
48
plugin was applied to filter and correct sequencing errors, infer amplicon sequence variants (ASVs), and remove chimeric sequences. Specifically, the first 15 bases of both forward and reverse reads were trimmed to remove primers and low-quality regions, while forward and reverse reads were truncated at 240 bp and 220 bp, respectively to retain high-quality regions. This procedure ensured the removal of sequencing errors while preserving high-resolution ASVs for downstream taxonomic and diversity analyses.
Taxonomy assignment
: To minimize sequencing noise and consolidate similar sequences,
de novo
operational taxonomic unit (OTU) clustering was performed using VSEARCH within QIIME 2. Sequences were clustered at 99% sequence identity, grouping highly similar sequences into the same OTU. For bacterial microbiome analysis, filtered amplicon sequence variants (ASVs) were taxonomically classified using the QIIME 2 feature-classifier plugin, which applies a naïve Bayes classifier trained on the SILVA reference database.
57
SILVA is a widely recognized, high-quality ribosomal RNA (rRNA) reference database that enables accurate taxonomic annotation of microbial communities.
52
Taxonomic assignment was performed using the pre-trained naïve Bayes classifier based on SILVA release 138, with a 99% sequence identity threshold. The resulting OTU tables and taxonomy assignments were integrated into two phyloseq objects
58
in .RData format for downstream statistical and visualization analyses. The phyloseq framework facilitates streamlined microbiome data management, supporting efficient implementation of alpha diversity, beta diversity, and differential abundance analyses.
Alpha Diversity Analysis
: Alpha diversity was assessed using two metrics: the Shannon index and the Chao1 richness estimator. The Shannon index incorporates both species richness and evenness, providing a measure of diversity within each sample, while the Chao1 index estimates species richness, particularly accounting for rare taxa. These metrics were computed for each sample using R (v4.4.1) vegan package, and differences in alpha diversity were evaluated between the two groups. Statistical significance was assessed using the Mann-Whitney U test, a non-parametric method suitable for comparing distributions between two independent groups. Multiple testing corrections were applied where appropriate to control for false discovery rates.
Beta Diversity Analysis:
Beta diversity was assessed to compare microbial community composition across samples using the weighted UniFrac distance metric,
59
a phylogenetic-based measure that accounts for both taxonomic relatedness and relative abundance. The weighted UniFrac distances were computed using the GUniFrac package in R. To evaluate differences in microbial community composition between HIV+ and HIV− groups, permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA) was performed on pairwise weighted UniFrac distances using the adonis2 function from the ape package in R, with 999 permutations. To visualize the beta diversity patterns, principal coordinate analysis (PCoA) was conducted on the weighted UniFrac distance matrix using the cmd scale function from the R base package. The first two principal coordinate axes were plotted to capture the major sources of variation in microbial community structure across samples.
Differential Abundance Analysis
:
To identify microbial taxa that significantly differed between the two groups, differential abundance analysis was conducted using the Linear Discriminant Analysis Effect Size (LEfSe) method.
60
LEfSe is a statistical approach designed to detect biologically meaningful differences in microbiome composition by integrating non-parametric statistical tests with Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA). LEfSe analysis was performed using the microbiome Marker package in R. For microbiome data, the Wilcoxon rank-sum test (for two-group comparisons) and the Kruskal-Wallis test (for multi-group comparisons) were applied with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. The LDA score cutoff was set to 2.0 to ensure the selection of strongly discriminative microbial features. To control for multiple testing, p-values were adjusted using the False Discovery Rate (FDR) correction. To visualize the hierarchical structure of microbial biomarkers identified by LEfSe, a taxonomy tree was constructed using the BAZE package. This representation facilitates the interpretation of taxonomic relationships among differentially abundant microbial taxa. For the key microbial markers identified through LEfSe analysis, we further examined their association with Control and PLWH groups using the Wilcoxon rank-sum test. To ensure robust statistical inference, p-values were adjusted using both FDR correction and Bonferroni adjustment, minimizing the risk of false-positive findings. This stringent approach enhances the reliability of conclusions regarding the significance of microbial differences between the groups in comparison.
